INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
Amicus curiae Federation for American Immigration
Reform (“FAIR”) is a nonprofit corporation and
membership organization that was founded in 1979 and
has its principal place of business in Washington, D.C.
FAIR’s mission is to advocate for immigration policy that
is in America’s best interests. FAIR has been involved in
more than 100 legal cases since 1980, either as a party or
amicus curiae , with the aim of advancing this mission. 1
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
This Court should reverse the court below. As a
criminal alien, Respondent (“G.M.”) has no fundamental
liberty interest in being released from custody into the
United States pending his removal proceedings. Congress
has reasonably concluded that mandatory detention
pending removal serves the purposes of protecting the
public from dangerous criminal aliens and ensuring the
presence of criminal aliens at their removal proceedings
and ultimately their removal from the country. Because
mandatory detention of such criminal aliens passes
rational-basis review, and therefore does not raise
substantive due process concerns, the court below erred
in ordering a bond hearing.
Indeed, the duration of mandatory detention under
8 U.S.C. § 1226(c) is entirely in the hands of the criminal
1. Pursuant to Rule 37.6, counsel for amicus authored this

2
alien charged with removability. Criminal aliens who
choose to contest their removability must remain in
custody, but such aliens can immediately bring their
detention to an end by conceding removability and
returning to their home country. Because the duration
of detention is in the hands of criminal aliens, prolonged
detention under § 1226(c) does not violate the Due Process
Clause, and this Court should therefore reverse the
judgment below.
ARGUMENT
I. Criminal aliens have no constitutional liberty
interest in being released into the United States
and are therefore not entitled to a bond hearing
under the Due Process Clause.
There is no question that the United States has a right
inherent in its sovereignty to defend itself from foreign
dangers by controlling the admission of aliens. “It is an
accepted maxim of international law that every sovereign
nation has the power, as inherent in sovereignty, and
essential to self-preservation, to forbid the entrance of
foreigners within its dominions, or to admit them only in
such	cases	 and	 upon	such	conditions	 as	 it	may	see	 fit	to
prescribe.” Nishimura Ekiu v. United States , 142 U.S.
651, 659 (1892); see also Galvan v. Press , 347 U.S. 522,
531 (1954) (“Policies pertaining to the entry of aliens and
their right to remain here are . . . entrusted exclusively
to Congress”). This Court “has repeatedly emphasized
that over no conceivable subject is the legislative power of
Congress more complete than it is over the admission of
aliens.” Fiallo v. Bell, 430 U.S. 787, 792 (1977) (quotation
omitted).

3
Exercising this sovereign prerogative, Congress has
enacted a comprehensive and detailed statutory scheme
regulating immigration, the purpose of which is to
prevent and deter illegal immigration and provide for the
removal of certain aliens. 2 In enacting 8 U.S.C. § 1226(c),
Congress mandated that certain criminal aliens be
detained without the possibility of a bond hearing except
for narrow witness-protection purposes not applicable
here. This statute provides that the government “shall
take into custody” aliens who have committed certain
criminal offenses, aliens who are removable on grounds
relating to terrorist activity, or certain inadmissible aliens
who have been charged with, been arrested for, been
convicted of, or admit having committed certain offenses.
8 U.S.C. § 1226(c)(1)(A)-(E). Congress has provided that
such criminal aliens shall be detained “pending a decision
on whether the alien is to be removed from the United
States,” 8 U.S.C. § 1226(a), and that they may be released
from custody only for certain witness-protection purposes
and only if the alien demonstrates that he or she “will not
pose a danger to the safety of other persons or of property
and is likely to appear for any scheduled proceeding.”
8 U.S.C. § 1226(c)(4). Thus, one of the conditions that
Congress has established for aliens to remain at liberty in
the United States is to avoid committing certain crimes.
If	an	alien	commits	a	specified	crime,	he	has	forfeited	his
right to remain at liberty in the United States.
2.	 Congress	 has	 specified	 numerous	 classes	 of	 aliens	 who
are removable from the United States, such as aliens who
enter illegally, commit certain crimes, violate the terms of
their status (visa overstays), obtain admission through fraud or
misrepresentation, vote unlawfully, become a public charge, and
whose work would undermine wages or working conditions of
American workers. See generally  8  U.S.C.	 §§	 1182(a)	 (defining
inadmissible	aliens)	and	1227(a)	(defining	deportable	aliens).

4
The Constitution prohibits the federal government
from “depriv[ing]” a “person” of “life, liberty, or property,
without due process of law.” U.S. Const. amend. V. This
Court has recognized two types of due-process claims.
See Department of State v. Muñoz , 602 U.S. 899, 910
(2024). A procedural-due-process claim takes as given the
substantive determinations that would justify a deprivation
of life, liberty, or property, but challenges the “adequacy
of the[] procedures” for making those determinations.
Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319, 335 (1976). In contrast,
a substantive-due-process claim challenges the substance
of the determinations themselves, arguing that they are
inadequate to justify the deprivation “ at all .” Reno v.
Flores, 507 U.S. 292, 302 (1993).
The court below held that such criminal aliens have a
“significant	liber ty	interest”	to	be	free	from	“unreasonably
prolonged” detention in the United States while removal
proceedings are pending. Black v. Dir. Thomas Decker ,
10 3  F. 4th 133, 148-51 (2d Cir. 2024). The court further held
that due process entitles criminal aliens to individualized
bond hearings once their detentions become unreasonably
prolonged and that the government bears the burden at
such a hearing to show, by clear and convincing evidence,
the need for continued detention. Id. at 155-58. The court
erred in reaching both determinations.
Because § 1226(c) mandates detention based solely on
a	determination	 that	the	alien	has	committed	 a	specified
crime or is removable on grounds relating to terrorist
activity,	procedural	due	process	is	satisfied	if	an	adequate
procedure permits a criminal alien to challenge whether he
is subject to § 1226(c)’s mandatory detention scheme. See
Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill , 470 U.S. 532, 541

5
(1985) (“[T]he Due Process Clause provides that certain
substantive rights—life, liberty, and property—cannot
be deprived except pursuant to constitutionally adequate
procedures.”). Here, even though G.M. does not dispute
that he is subject to § 1226(c)’s mandatory detention
scheme, Black, 103 F .4th at 142 (“G.M. agree[s] … that
section 1226(c) applies to [him]”), there is no question that
adequate procedural protections are in place.
As the government points out, Brief for Petitioners
(“Pet. Br.”) at 6-7, a criminal alien may challenge whether
he falls within § 1226(c)’s ambit at a hearing before an
immigration judge. See 8 C.F .R. § 1003.19(h)(2)(ii); Matter
of Joseph, 22 I&N Dec. 799, 805-807 (BIA 1999); Matter
of Kotliar, 24 I&N Dec. 124, 126-127 (BIA 2007). “At the
hearing, the detainee may avoid mandatory detention by
demonstrating that he is not an alien, was not convicted
of the predicate crime, or that [the government] is
otherwise substantially unlikely to establish that he is in
fact subject to mandatory detention.” Demore v. Hyung
Joon Kim, 538 U.S. 510, 514 n.3 (2003). The criminal alien
or the government may appeal an adverse decision to the
Board of Immigration Appeals. 8 C.F .R. §§ 236.1(d)(3),
1236.1(d)(3).
Thus, this case turns on whether mandatory
detention under § 1226(c) comports with substantive
due process. Substantive due process claims require a
“careful description of the asserted fundamental liberty
interest.” Washington v. Glucksberg , 521 U.S. 702, 721
(1997) (quotation omitted). The court below described the
liberty interest at stake as “the interest in being free from
imprisonment.” Black, 103 F .4th at 151 (quotation omitted).
A more precise description of the right asserted, however,

6
is the right to be released from custody into the United
States pending completion of removal proceedings. 3 Cf.
Dep’t of State v. Muñoz , 602 U.S. 899, 909-11 (2024)
(redefining	a	petitioner’s	asserted	“right	to	marriage”	as	a
narrower “right to have her noncitizen husband enter (and
remain in) the United States”); Dep’t of Homeland Sec. v.
Thuraissigiam , 591 U.S. 103, 119 (2020) (distinguishing
between a right to release and the right to release into
the United States—“[w]hile respondent does not claim an
entitlement to release, the Government is happy to release
him—provided the release occurs in the cabin of a plane
bound for [the alien’s native country]”).
But G.M. has no fundamental right to freedom from
custody pending removal proceedings. “[P]rior to 1907
there was no provision permitting bail for any aliens during
the pendency of their deportation proceedings.” Demore,
538 U.S. at 523 n.7 (citing Immigration Act of 1907, Pub.
L. 59-96, 34 Stat. 898, 905 (Feb. 20, 1907)) (emphasis in
original). Thus, any right to seek release pending removal
proceedings is not “objectively, deeply rooted in this
Nation’s history and tradition” and cannot be a substantive
due process right. Glucksberg, 521 U.S. at 720-21.
Because criminal aliens have no substantive due
process right to be released from custody into the United
States pending removal proceedings, their detention
3. The government suggests that “the right being asserted is
not a right to be free from detention,” nor “a right to be at liberty
in the United States,” but instead “the right of an inadmissible
or deportable alien, detained pending a decision on removal, to a
bond hearing—followed by his release into the United States if
there	is	no	determination	 that	he	presents	a	flight	risk	or	danger.”
Pet. Br. at 30.

7
is subject only to rational-basis review. Id. at 728. And
this Court has already determined that the mandatory
detention scheme under § 1226(c) meets that standard.
Demore, 538 U.S. at 528 (“The evidence Congress had
before it certainly supports the approach it selected [i.e.,
§ 1226(c)’s mandatory detention scheme] even if other,
hypothetical studies might have suggested different
courses of action.”).
In sum, criminal aliens subject to § 1226(c)’s
mandatory detention scheme have no constitutional right
to bond hearings pending removal proceedings. Congress
has rationally concluded that mandatory detention serves
the purposes of protecting the public from dangerous
criminal aliens and ensuring the presence of criminal
aliens at their removal proceedings and ultimately their
removal from the country. Because criminal aliens have
no fundamental right to freedom within the United States
pending removal, the court below erred in grafting bond
hearings onto Congress’s mandatory detention scheme.
II.	 Even	 if	criminal	 aliens	have	a	“significant	liberty
interest” to be free from “unreasonably prolonged”
detention, G.M. can choose to avoid prolonged
detention by accepting removal and returning to
his native country.
Congress declined to set a temporal limit for detention
under § 1226(c), and to the extent that detention of a
criminal alien becomes prolonged, it is the result of the
criminal alien’s choice to remain in the United States to
contest his removal. 4 In other words, “an alien detained
4. As the government notes in its brief, Pet. Br. at 10 n.4, the
government prioritizes the adjudication of removal proceedings

8
under § 1226(c) ‘has the keys in his pocket’ and can ‘end
his detention immediately’ by ‘withdrawing his defense . . .
and returning to his native land.’” Banyee v. Garland, 115
F .4th 928, 933 (8th Cir. 2024) (quoting Parra v. Perryman,
172 F .3d 954, 958 (7th Cir. 1999)) (alterations omitted); cf.
Kiyemba v. Obama, 605 F .3d 1046, 1052 (D.C. Cir. 2010) (J.
Rogers, concurring) (“Petitioners’ claim of constitutional
entitlement to release in the continental United States
pending resettlement abroad has thus been overtaken
by events: Petitioners hold the keys to their release
from Guantanamo for resettlement in an ‘appropriate’
country.”). As this Court observed in Thuraissigiam , 591
U.S. at 119 (“[T]he Government is happy to release [the
detained alien]—provided the release occurs in the cabin
of a plane bound for [the alien’s native country].”). Because
the government would be happy to remove a criminal alien
and thereby release him from custody, the duration of
mandatory detention is entirely up to the criminal alien
charged with removal. Under § 1226(c), Congress has
determined that such criminal aliens shall be detained
only so long as it takes to complete removal proceedings. If
a criminal alien declines to contest his removal, detention
authority under § 1226(c) comes to an end.
Furthermore, there is no risk that a criminal alien
will	 be	detained	 indefinitely	 even	if	he	does	not	concede
removability. In Zadvydas v. Davis , this Court held that
an	 alien’s	 detention	 may	 not	 continue	 indefinitely.	 533
U.S. 678, 690-99 (2001); see also id.  at 701 (“[A]n alien
for detained aliens. Accordingly, removal proceedings for criminal
aliens detained under § 1226(c) are generally adjudicated much
quicker than non-detained alien cases, thereby greatly reducing
the duration of mandatory detention.

9
may	be	held	in	confinement	until	it	has	been	determined
that	 there	 is	 no	 significant	 likelihood	 of	 removal	 in	 the
reasonably foreseeable future.”). This Court has already
“distinguished § 1226(c) from the statutory provision in
Zadvydas by pointing out that detention under § 1226(c)
has	‘a	definite	termination	point’:	the	conclusion	of	removal
proceedings. 	 …[T]hat	 ‘definite	 termination 	 point’—and
not some arbitrary time limit devised by courts—marks
the end of the Government’s detention authority under
§ 1226(c).” Jennings v. Rodriguez , 583 U.S. 281, 304
(2018) (quoting Demore, 538 U.S. at 529). Thus, although
Zadvydas  does not extend to § 1226(c)’s mandatory
detention prior to the completion of removal proceedings,
which this Court has squarely held to be “a constitutionally
permissible part of [the removal] process,” Demore, 538
U.S. at 531, Zadvydas does ensure that any period of postremoval detention will not be unconstitutionally prolonged.

10
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, the judgment below should
be reversed.
Respectfully submitted,
